name: Omar Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I work at a big discount supermarket on the industrial estate, the warehouse kind where the stock sits on pallets in the aisles. Three days a week I'm on the tills, and we scan fast, they time us, about thirty items a minute. Two nights a week I'm on the night-fill crew, breaking down pallets and filling the shelves before the six o'clock open.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the night crew, it's five of us with the radio on and nobody watching the scan rate. The tills wear me out, the timer and the beeping and the target, my wrist aches by Thursday. I live with my girlfriend Amira, she's a receptionist at a dental practice, and we're saving for a deposit on a house. My dad was a bricklayer, and he still says I should have done a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with it, there's work to do. At the shop the lads would say the same, nobody on the night crew cared about AI anyway. I'd probably say it to my dad over Sunday dinner, that the clever people got it wrong again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't change my real problem, which is the house. We've got about four months of bills saved and a deposit fund that grows slower than prices. My job's fine, the discount places are busy because people are skint, but fine isn't getting us a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both my shifts and ask for a third night if they've got it, because nights pay a bit more. Amira and I would keep putting four hundred a month in the deposit fund. I'd also look again at the electrician apprenticeship at the college, because my dad's right, a trade gets you further than a till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit stuck. Like running on the spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long until you'd have the deposit at that rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four years, if prices don't jump, and they always jump. I worked it out on the AI app on my phone once, put in the numbers, and it said 2030. I closed the app and went for a run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's stopped you doing the apprenticeship so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. An apprentice wage the first year is less than I get now, and we'd lose a year on the deposit. Amira says do it anyway, she says she'll carry us for a year, but I don't like that.

say: **Good, let's get on** with it; there's work to do.
The **clever people** got it wrong again, I'd tell my dad over Sunday dinner.
think: His real problem is the **house deposit**, growing slower than prices.
His job is **fine** because discount shops are busy, but fine won't buy a house.
do: Keep both shifts and ask for **a third night**, which pays more.
Keep putting **four hundred a month** into the deposit fund with Amira.
Look again at the college **electrician apprenticeship**.
feel: **Steady** but stuck, like running on the spot.
S0.quote: My job's fine, the discount places are busy because people are skint, but fine isn't getting us a house.
fieldNote: His pressure is **housing**, not AI; the deposit looks about four years away.
Pride stops him letting Amira **carry the household** during an apprenticeship.
Father's voice about **trades** shapes his thinking.

steps.text: Ask the night manager for a third night-fill shift
Keep paying four hundred a month into the house deposit fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that'll feel it, and a few of those people might finally see what a real day's work is. That's a bit harsh, I know. At work I'd say the shelves still need filling, and I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Amira I'd worry about. Booking appointments, answering the phone, sending reminders, that's exactly the list on your card. My girlfriend's dental practice could get by with an AI on the phone and one person at the desk, and she's one of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push us to do the apprenticeship plan now, not later, while there's still two incomes. I'd apply for the college's electrician apprenticeship for September and keep a night-fill shift at the weekend on top. I'd tell Amira to ask her practice manager straight out about the phones, and to look at the dental nurse course, because that's hands in mouths, not phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not for me so much as for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you didn't like Amira carrying you. Has that changed here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I suppose it flips. If her job's the one at risk, then I need to be on a better wage sooner, and an apprenticeship is the way. Funny, the thing that stopped me is the thing that pushes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if it's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My football subs and the gym, that's forty a month. Then the car insurance goes to the cheaper one, and we stop the takeaway on Saturdays. The deposit fund I'd try not to touch.

say: The **office jobs** will feel it, and maybe see what a real day's work is.
The **shelves still need filling**, I'd say at work.
think: Girlfriend Amira's **reception job** matches the card's list almost exactly.
Her dental practice could cut to **one person** at the desk, and she's one of two.
do: Apply for the college **electrician apprenticeship** this September.
Keep a weekend **night-fill** shift on top of the apprentice wage.
Cut football subs, gym and takeaways, about **forty a month** plus more.
feel: **Anxious**, more for the household than for himself.
S1.quote: My girlfriend's dental practice could get by with an AI on the phone and one person at the desk, and she's one of two.
fieldNote: The risk lands on the **other earner**, which flips his pride about being carried.
Starts with a **harsh line** about office workers, then softens it himself.
Plans rest on **trades and apprenticeships**, in line with his outlook.

steps.text: Apply for the college electrician apprenticeship starting in September
Keep one weekend night-fill shift at the discount supermarket
Drop football subs, the gym and Saturday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless and somebody in charge should have stopped it. At work everyone would be on their phones about it. I'd say what my dad says, that a man needs to be able to do something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for both of us. Amira's desk job goes almost straight away in 2028, and the robots come for my tills and shelves around 2031. An apprenticeship takes four years, so I'd only just finish as the robots arrive, and I don't know if they'll want new electricians or robot ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the apprenticeship straight away, because wiring old houses is messy and I reckon that's the last thing a robot learns. We'd stop the deposit fund and keep that money as a cushion, about nine thousand. And we'd probably move in with my parents to cut the rent, which I'd hate but it's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The house we wanted would float off down the river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not her fault and we'll be all right, even if I wasn't sure. Then I'd say we're moving in with my mum and dad for a bit. She gets on with my mum, thank God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there's nothing else. I'd rather do three night shifts than queue for a handout. But if they paid for apprenticeships, I'd take that, that's helping people work.

say: It's **reckless**, and somebody in charge should have stopped it.
A man needs to do something with **his hands**, as my dad says.
think: Amira's **desk job** goes almost at once in 2028; his tills and shelves around 2031.
A four-year **apprenticeship** would only finish as the robots arrive.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** at once, betting old-house wiring is the last thing robots learn.
Turn the **deposit fund**, about nine thousand, into an emergency cushion.
Move in with **his parents** to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like watching the house they wanted float away.
S2.quote: The house we wanted would float off down the river.
fieldNote: Both earners hit in sequence: **thinking AI** first for Amira, robots later for him.
Still backs a **trade**, but doubts the timing honestly.
Accepts **family support** readily, state support only if it funds work.

steps.text: Start the four-year electrician apprenticeship straight away
Turn the nine-thousand deposit fund into an emergency cushion
Move in with his parents to cut the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to learn a trade, so get learning. At work I'd tell the younger lads on nights to sign up for something, not wait. My dad would say he told me so, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it fits the apprenticeship almost exactly. Four years and I'm a qualified electrician by 2030, a year before AGI, and robots don't come till 2034. That gives me four or five years of good wages to get the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next September and keep two weekend night-fill shifts, which keeps us about where we are now. Amira would do the dental nurse course while she still has the reception wage. We'd keep the deposit fund going, smaller, maybe two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels like a plan instead of a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is two night shifts on top of an apprenticeship realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, yes, I'm twenty-seven, not fifty. My mate Kris did nights while he did his plumbing course and he says it nearly killed him. So maybe one night by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Amira's course doesn't lead anywhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm the earner for a while, and the house waits. I'd rather that than both of us on tills. We'd manage, people have managed on less.

say: **Five years** is enough to learn a trade, so get learning.
I'd tell the **younger lads** on nights to sign up now.
think: The apprenticeship **fits almost exactly**: qualified by 2030, before AGI.
Robots in 2034 leave **four or five years** of good wages for the house.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** next September with two weekend night shifts.
Back Amira through the **dental nurse course** while she still has her wage.
Keep the deposit fund at **two hundred** a month.
feel: **Worried**, but it feels like a plan instead of a fall.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to learn a trade, so get learning.
fieldNote: Times his training precisely against the **three-year robot gap**.
Accepts being the **sole earner** for a while, reversing his earlier pride.
Still anxious: the till job ends and Amira's **income is at risk**.

steps.text: Start the electrician apprenticeship next September
Keep two weekend night-fill shifts during the first years
Cut the deposit fund payment to two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't sort themselves out has only themselves to blame. That's what my dad would say. At work I'd say it more kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's comfortable for me. I'd be a qualified electrician long before 2036, and robots in 2039 are thirteen years off. Amira has time to switch to nursing. The house still worries me more than robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, but I'd wait a year to get the deposit higher first, maybe start in 2028. I'd keep the tills and nights until then. Once qualified, I'd try to work for myself, because a small electrician with his own van is what my dad always wanted for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy still, because of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people only have themselves to blame. Do you really think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, with ten years. But I'd think of the older women on our tills, like Brenda who's sixty. She can't do a four-year apprenticeship, so it's not her fault, and I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI in your own electrician business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the quotes and invoices, probably, everyone will. Amira already uses it to write the practice's reminder texts. I'd use AI for the paperwork and keep the screwdriver for me.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, and people mostly have only themselves to blame.
At work I'd say it **more kindly**.
think: He'd be a **qualified electrician** long before 2036.
The **house** still worries him more than robots do.
Amira has years to **switch to nursing** before her desk job goes.
do: Wait a year to **build the deposit**, then start the apprenticeship in 2028.
Aim for **his own van** and small electrician business once qualified.
feel: **Mostly fine**, still a bit uneasy about the house.
S4.quote: I'd use AI for the paperwork and keep the screwdriver for me.
fieldNote: A long warning makes him **delay** rather than rush, to protect the deposit.
His tough line on **personal responsibility** softens for an older colleague, Brenda.
Steady with tech: happy to use AI for **paperwork** once it's normal.

steps.text: Start the electrician apprenticeship in 2028 after building the deposit
Keep tills and night-fill shifts until the apprenticeship starts
Use AI for quotes and invoices in his own electrician business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Amira and I would both lose our jobs inside three years and the house would be gone for good. What would help is apprenticeships that pay a proper wage, so a man of twenty-seven with rent can afford to train. That's help I'd take with my head up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the night crew. Five of us, and none of us has a plan except me, and mine is only half a plan. Someone should be talking to the people who fill the shelves at four in the morning.

headlineQuote: Someone should be talking to the people who fill the shelves at four in the morning.
portrait: Omar, 27, works the **tills and night fill** at a warehouse-style discount supermarket and lives with Amira, a dental receptionist.
His real worry is the **house deposit**, which grows slower than prices even when AI changes nothing.
In every AI picture he worries first about Amira's **desk job**, which thinking AI reaches before his hands-on work.
He trusts **trades**, and an electrician apprenticeship is his answer, timed against when robots arrive.
He prefers **family help** to handouts, but would take paid apprenticeships with his head up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Amira could lose work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** that pay a proper wage, so people with rent can afford to train.
